catalog_quote: Kashaya, a Pomoan language of northern California, has a complex but almost entirely regular system for assigning stress (Oswalt 1961, 1988). The basic analysis involves iambic feet beginning at the left edge, with iambic lengthening of stressed open syllables (Buckley 1994a,b); however, vowels located in a large class of “outer” suffixes, such as -mela below, do not undergo lengthening. Main stress falls on the first foot; secondary stress is not transcribed in the sources, but iterative feet are required to account for iambic lengthening and other phenomena. In words with a monosyllabic root, the first iamb is fully at the left edge, and stress falls on an initial heavy, otherwise the second syllable. ... In words beginning with a disyllabic or longer root, such as /tumhu/ ‘buy’, or any word containing an instrumental prefix, as in /di-hyoqʰ/ ‘shake and fall’, the first syllable is ex…
sweep_summary: Two title-matched items, both already in the per-language bibliography. (1) Buckley 2017 'Global effects in Kashaya prosodic structure' (Glottolog wrongly adds editors Gribanova & Shih as authors) was already held by the project as the author's open preprint and was read: it states the left-to-right, weight-sensitive iambic system (initial heavy else 2nd; with default initial extrametricality heavy 2nd else 3rd; (Cv:) foot skipping and Foot Flipping push accent to the 4th/5th syllable) — confirms the catalog's weight/left-edge coding and refines the placement rule with the Foot Flipping clause. (2) Oswalt 1988 'The floating accent of Kashaya' (Mouton de Gruyter, 611-622) could not be read: the DOI sits behind a De Gruyter bot wall with no abstract, archive. bibliographic records (WALS 14A/15A/16A: no fixed stress, left-oriented one of first three, long vowel or coda consonant; Buckley's citations for left-edge iambs and iambic lengthening) are consistent with the catalog. Medium acquisition priority: it is Oswalt's own primary statement of the accent shift, reachable through the Harvard library catalogue/ProQuest chapter record per the prior our access check record, but Buckley's held restatements (1997, 2014/2017, 2019, 2021) already carry the analysis with Oswalt's data. No new source supersedes the catalog's deciding Buckley 2014 (symmetry) + 2018 source.

new_statements.quote: Metrical structure in Kashaya is iambic, constructed from left to right in a stepwise approach (Buckley 1994b) or aligned to the left in a constraint-based theory (Buckley 1997). As expected under this basic pattern, stress falls on the first syllable if it is heavy, otherwise on the second. [...] A central fact about Kashaya stress is that the first syllable is extrametrical by default (Buckley 1994a,b) [...] As a result, the vowels that undergo Iambic Lengthening are shifted one syllable to the right, and the stress occurs on a heavy second syllable, otherwise on the third syllable.

new_statements.reading: weight-sensitive, left-edge iambic stress: initial heavy else 2nd syllable for monosyllabic unprefixed roots; with default initial extrametricality (disyllabic or prefixed roots) heavy 2nd else 3rd; a leftmost (Cv:) foot or a flipped (CvCv:) foot is skipped, pushing accent to the 3rd/4th or 4th/5th syllable, so stress can land on any of the first five syllables. Heavy = closed syllable or long vowel. This confirms the catalog's classification weight, left edge, CVV+CVC heavy, and refines the placement rule by adding the Foot Flipping clause (reach to the 5th syllable), which the catalog's deciding quotation does not mention.

new_statements.quote: Feet are iambic, i.e. right-headed and quantity-sensitive, and are constructed from the left edge of the domain (Buckley 1994; Oswalt 1961, 1988). [...] In (25) and (26), stress falls on the second syllable if it is /CVC/, and otherwise on the third syllable. [...] The leftmost foot is normally the location of primary stress, defined here as an abstract metrical prominence that correlates with the foot head. The main cue for this prominence is a pitch accent, i.e. a raised F0. [...] If the leftmost foot is nonbranching /CV:/, accent is shifted to the following foot. As a result, accent then falls on the third syllable if heavy, otherwise the fourth.

new_statements.relation_note: Same system as the existing statement from Buckley 2017 (left-edge quantity-sensitive iambs, initial heavy/2nd or 2nd heavy/3rd, CV: shift, foot flipping to the 5th syllable) and as the catalog's weight / left-edge / CVV+CVC-heavy classification; adds that the cue is a pitch accent, that no secondary stress is transcribed, and that the placement domain is frequently a multi-word accent phrase with optional grouping and deaccentuation of short phrases. The catalog record's rule field is empty, so this supplies a rule where the catalog has none.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Left-to-right quantity-sensitive iambic footing; the leftmost foot's head carries the primary stress, cued by a pitch accent (raised F0). With the default initial-syllable extrametricality (words with a prefix or a polysyllabic root) stress falls on the 2nd syllable if closed (heavy), otherwise on the 3rd; extrametricality is blocked for monosyllabic unprefixed roots (the root must be footed), so there stress is on the 1st syllable if heavy, else the 2nd. If the first footed syllable is CV: (underlying or from vowel coalescence, even when surface-shortened in a closed syllable) the accent shifts to the next foot (3rd if heavy, else 4th); foot flipping (/CV:CV/ surfacing as CVCV:) pushes accent to the 5th syllable. Heavy = closed syllable or long vowel.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None transcribed: 'Although iterative metrical feet are well motivated by the location of lengthened vowels, there is not clear evidence of secondary phonetic prominences beyond the main stress, so only the pitch accent is transcribed.' (p. 10)
new_statements.exceptions: (a) Extrametricality blocked for monosyllabic unprefixed roots (p. 9). (b) Accent shift off a nonbranching CV: leftmost foot, including opaque cases where the long vowel is shortened in a closed syllable (pp. 10-11, exx. 27-29). (c) Foot flipping puts accent on the 5th syllable (pp. 10-11, ex. 30). (d) Certain later suffixes never undergo iambic lengthening. (e) The domain is often larger than the word: 'stress is quite often assigned to phrasal constituents that consist of more than one word at both the M and P levels of analysis' (p. 5); an accent phrase of two M-Words is footed as one domain, often putting the accent on the second word (sec. 11.3, exx. 31-32), grouping is optional except in reduplicated verbs (sec. 11.4). (f) Short accent phrases are often deaccented (Oswalt's 'accent suppression', pp. 15-16).
new_statements.identity_note: Buckley 2021 describes Kashaya (Southwestern Pomo) of northern California, drawing on Oswalt's 1961, 1964 and 2005 data and the author's own fieldwork; no sub-dialect is distinguished.

The domain in which feet are created is a prosodic phrase or P-PHRASE, which may consist of just one or of several words. ... Many p-phrases lack a surface accent due to ACCENT SUPPRESSION, or the non-realization of a stressed syllable as accented. ... The general avoidance of this overlap may have arisen because the accent is less perceptible when it occurs too close to the intonational boundary tone.

sources.note: Defines Kashaya ACCENT as a tone associated with (some) metrical prominences, distinct from STRESS (foot-head prominence); feet are built across a multiword p-phrase, the leftmost foot head of a p-phrase may surface with the (pitch) accent; accents can be suppressed ('accent suppression', after Oswalt 1961) or retracted leftward; IP-final intonational contours/boundary tone (Oswalt 1961) make phrase-final accents dispreferred; corpus counts (11,435 accent-marked p-phrases in 9,996 intonational phrases) and an alignment (OT) analysis of p-phrasing vs XP edges. No lexical tone.
